newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Economists see US rate rise near mid-year.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Economists see US rate rise near mid-year.

text.p: The majority of U.S. economists in a Reuters poll forecast the Federal Reserve's next interest rate move will be a tightening and that it will take place near the middle of the year.

"The fundamental issue is how long can inflation remain benign when growth remains fairly strong," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc, who projected a tightening in the second half of the year.
"If the labor market continues to tighten and wage rates continue to rise, sooner or later that rise in wage rates will lift employment costs and, therefore, prices," he said.
Lieberman said the Fed is unlikely to act in anticipation of higher prices, but is likely to respond fairly quickly at the first sign price increases are accelerating.
Such signs most likely are a few months away, most analysts said.

"We do not expect the Fed to raise rates at the February meeting," said Raymond Worseck, chief economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "We expect the Federal funds rate to be pushed up by a quarter to half a percent and it's more likely that that move would come in the second half of the year than in the first half."
Worseck said economic growth would taper off in the first quarter of 1997, alleviating any pressure on the Fed to raise rates.
"I don't believe we have an inflation problem," said D'Antonio. "I think inflation will be subdued and demand growth will moderate and the next interest-rate move move will most likely be down."
For now, the Fed will keep rates steady until they have determined a clear direction for the economy, D'Antonio said.
"Once they know that, that will determine which way they go and I think they ultimately will have to ease, rather than tighten."
What would hasten the day for an interest rate easing would be a rise in the unemployment rate, D'Antonio said.
To change the perception of a tight labor market, "we need to see a change in the unemployment rate," he said. "We need to see it rise."
D'Antonio said that, in the first half of 1997, demand will soften, production will slow and the labor market will soften.
